title: Tamsin and the Confession
premise: When a sealed confession letter arrives at the Marlowe Grand Hotel addressed to concierge Emrys Thornbury—postmarked the day after the funeral of its late owner, Sir Aldous Vane—Emrys realizes the letter names them as the only person who can prove the confession true. The letter claims Sir Aldous was murdered by one of his four heirs, and that the proof lies in a guest ledger hidden in plain sight within the hotel's own registry. Racing a murder trial already underway against the wrong suspect, Emrys decodes the ledger's cipher of room numbers and dates, uncovering a decades-old inheritance scheme built on a swapped birthright. In the end, Emrys exposes the true killer—the loyal hotel manager who poisoned Aldous to protect her own stolen inheritance—clearing the accused heir and choosing truth over the belonging the Vane family finally offered her.
about_author: Dominic Joubert is a former night auditor at a grand seaside hotel who spent years collecting the strange confessions guests make at 3 a.m. He writes mysteries from a converted bellhop's quarters, insisting that every lobby hides a story no one has checked out.

chapters.title: Postmarked After the Funeral
chapters.summary: Emrys Thornbury's POV. A rain-slicked morning at the Marlowe Grand; Emrys sorts the post and finds a confession letter addressed to them, postmarked the day after Sir Aldous Vane's funeral. The letter claims murder and promises proof in a ledger. Emotional beat: unease beneath professional composure.

chapters.title: The Letter That Names Me
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Reading the confession privately, Emrys learns the writer claims to have witnessed poisoning and insists only Emrys's memory of the guest registry can verify dates. The letter begs them to act before the trial. Beat: reluctant obligation; Emrys's pride in closing every case takes hold.

chapters.title: Four Heirs in Mourning
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Emrys observes the Vane heirs at the hotel's memorial tea—eldest son Casper, brittle daughter Ysolde, estranged nephew Rhys, and the accused ward, Mirabel. Each performs grief differently. Beat: Emrys catalogues tells, sensing every heir is hiding something.

chapters.title: A Registry of Small Lies
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Emrys pulls the old guest ledgers and notices dates around Sir Aldous's final week don't match staff schedules—rooms logged as occupied when they stood empty. Beat: the first hard clue; excitement sharpening into dread.

chapters.title: The Trial Opens Without Me
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Emrys and trial reports. Mirabel Vane's trial begins; the prosecution's timeline hinges on a dinner Emrys personally served—and remembers differently. Beat: Emrys realizes their own testimony could save or doom Mirabel.

chapters.title: Room 412, Always 412
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. The confession letter's odd phrasing—'the room that never changes'—leads Emrys to Room 412, booked every year on the same date for thirty years under shifting names. Beat: pattern recognition; the ledger is a cipher, not a record.

chapters.title: What the Night Staff Saw
chapters.summary: Night porter Bex's POV. Bex recalls the night Sir Aldous collapsed, including a figure on the service stairs and a teacup that vanished. Beat: corroborating witness found, but Bex is frightened and wants to forget.

chapters.title: The Manager Who Never Left
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Emrys interviews Odile Ferrant, the devoted manager who served the Vanes for forty years. Her loyalty seems unimpeachable—too unimpeachable. Beat: Emrys's instinct prickles against the hotel's most trusted face.

chapters.title: Cipher of Dates and Doors
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Cross-referencing Room 412's bookings with the ledger, Emrys finds a repeating sequence: every date maps to a family event—a birth, a death, a marriage. The ledger records an inheritance, not guests. Beat: the hidden structure revealed.

chapters.title: A Birthright Swapped
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. The cipher decodes to a thirty-year-old secret: the true eldest Vane child was swapped at birth, and the inheritance—and the murder motive—flow from it. Beat: the case inverts; the confession letter's author may be the swapped child.

chapters.title: The Letter Writer Surfaces
chapters.summary: Rhys Vane's POV. Rhys admits he sent the confession after finding his aunt Odile burning papers; he believes he is the swapped child and that Odile engineered the swap to control the estate. Beat: alliance formed, but Rhys's motive is inheritance, not justice.

chapters.title: Burning in the Boiler Room
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Emrys catches Odile destroying decades of ledgers; she claims housekeeping, but the burned pages match the missing cipher dates. Beat: open confrontation; Odile's mask slips just enough.

chapters.title: Mirabel's Silence
chapters.summary: Prison interview, Emrys's POV. Mirabel refuses a defense built on the ledger, insisting exposing the birthright secret would destroy the family she loves. Beat: loyalty versus truth made personal; Emrys must choose what justice means.

chapters.title: The Poisoner's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Emrys reconstructs the poisoning: foxglove from the hotel garden, administered across three dinners so no single dose kills—only someone with daily access to Aldous's tray. Beat: the suspect pool narrows to staff, not family.

chapters.title: A Key That Opens Everything
chapters.summary: Bex's POV. Bex produces a master key tagged to Odile's name, logged out the night of the collapse, and a teacup she hid rather than destroyed. Beat: physical evidence secured; danger now walks toward Emrys.

chapters.title: Threats at the Front Desk
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Emrys receives a warning: a reservation under a dead guest's name, a note in the cipher. Someone inside knows how close they are. Beat: fear; Emrys, the observer, becomes the observed.

chapters.title: The Second Confession
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Emrys decodes the final ledger entry: Odile Ferrant is the swapped child herself, raised as staff while her birthright was given away—and Aldous discovered it days before his death. Beat: motive fully revealed; the confession letter was Odile's own, unsent.

chapters.title: Offered a Place at the Table
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. The surviving heirs, desperate to avoid scandal, offer Emrys a permanent post and a place in the family's confidence—if the ledger disappears and Mirabel takes the fall. Beat: belonging dangled as the price of truth.

chapters.title: The Last Night Audit
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Emrys spends the night reconstructing every proof: cipher, key log, teacup, Bex's testimony—knowing dawn brings the trial's closing arguments. Beat: quiet, resolute preparation; the concierge's ledger of the case complete.

chapters.title: Closing Arguments and a Closed Case
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Emrys delivers the evidence to the court, walking the jury through the cipher aloud. Odile, watching from the gallery, does not run. Beat: climax; truth spoken in the one room that outranks the hotel.

chapters.title: What Odile Confessed
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. In a holding cell, Odile admits the poisoning and the swap, insisting she only took back what was stolen—until Aldous threatened to expose her and unmake her life's belonging. Beat: tragic confession; villain and victim entwined.

chapters.title: The Concierge Stays On
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Mirabel is freed; Rhys renounces his inheritance claim; the hotel, scarred but standing, asks Emrys to remain—not as family, but as its keeper of truths. Emrys files the case closed. Beat: resolution; loyalty and truth reconciled, belonging earned rather than inherited.
